title: New York’s First-Ever Retromobile Kicks Off Strong, but Paris Prevails

body_markdown:
The first Retromobile was an automotive flea market held 50 years ago in a disused train station in Paris. After a half-century of expanding upward and outward, becoming a fixture on the European classic-car show calendar, it has finally crossed the Atlantic to land in New York City, where the gates at the glass-enclosed Javits Center on Manhattan’s west side opened last Thursday for a four-day run.


Aaron Robinson


By Saturday, with the attached Gooding Christie’s auction busy liquidating piano man Billy Joel’s motorcycle collection and a heavy crowd that had paid $70 for a ticket to circulate among the 350 display cars and various vendors, the event appeared to be a success. Gerard Neveau, a former Formula 1 official who is now CEO of Retromobile New York, said the current three-year deal with Javits should give the event enough time to get its footing—perhaps even become the anchor of a weeklong Big Apple classic-car extravaganza with other auction companies and events joining in.


“The baby is born, well born. Now we have to grow up and, like a baby, next year we will have to learn to walk, and then the year after to speak, and then to run,” said Neveau.


Rétromobile Paris


Aaron Robinson


Rétromobile Paris


Aaron Robinson


Paris Retromobile is a multilayer classic car festival in February that is basically an indoor Hershey. Held in February at the Paris Exposition Center, it brings light to the depths of the gloomy Parisian winter for around 200,000 old-car enthusiasts who pay about $22 for a basic ticket. Almost everything is for sale in the show. At the top of the menu are the large dealers like London-based Fiskens and Girardo & Co. that retail ultra-high-end classics on expansive carpeted booths that resemble new-car auto show displays. In the middle tier are lifestyle companies that display art, models, tools, trailers, and other automotive paraphernalia. And at the grassroots level are booths for car clubs and small parts vendors, the vestiges of Retromobile in its original form.


Rétromobile Paris


Aaron Robinson


Rétromobile Paris


Aaron Robinson


Rétromobile Paris


Aaron Robinson


Paris runs six days and is a solid two days of entertainment for any enthusiast, assuming he or she is not a casual skimmer. It’s also where you can get your nerd on for the deep tracks from European car culture. A few years ago the main hall featured everything from a display of Peugeot concept cars from the past 60 years to a collection of Group B rally machines to a couple of Sherman tanks. Fancy joining the Facel Vega Club of France? Their booth was richly adorned with examples of the marque and expensive Facel Vega silk scarves for purchase.


“In New York we tried to do the same, but it doesn’t work like this,” said Neveau, who two years ago started planning the expansion to Manhattan, where, he says, everything is more expensive than Paris. “We found immediately the capacity to build the \[top\] level with the right people, the high level of people, and now we are looking to build the ground floor.”


Aaron Robinson


One of the high-level people is Mark Hyman of Hyman Limited in Saint Louis, a prominent dealer of exotic and esoteric classics that had prime placement in Javits for a dozen cars right by the entrance. “When they told me in Paris last year that they wanted to do this, I said yes, because this is what we do, this is who we are,” said Hyman. “These are the types of cars we showcase and we wanted to show the world.”


Hyman pitches a tent at Hershey every year but otherwise there haven’t been any indoor classic-car events like Retromobile in the U.S. (one in Los Angeles folded after a few years). “We have a 70,000-square-foot building with 200 amazing cars,” said Hyman, “but most of our interaction is on the phone or by website, so we don’t have the opportunity for face-to-face as much. This is our opportunity.” He said his firm had also sold a few cars off the show floor in New York, which helped make the commitment worthwhile.


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


While having about the same number of cars on display as Paris, Retromobile New York, with its 100 exhibitors, was more concentrated on the big dealers and auction houses. The single largest user of the 400,000 square feet of space was for cars and motorcycles relatred to the adjoining Gooding Christie’s auction. Also part of the show was a gallery from New Jersey art-car collector Larry Warsh that included cars adorned by famous artists such as Jeff Koons and the late Keith Haring, and a small movie-car section featured the Ghostbusters Caddy, the Batmobile, and a Back-to-the-Future DeLorean.


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


A few lifestyle firms displayed items such as $80,000 custom car-hauling trailers and luxury motorhomes, and there were a smattering of dealers of art, models, and vintage watches. One of the star vehicles of the show was a towering red GM Futurliner, owned by local collector Howard Kroplick and restored to its original 1939 bubble-canopy spec. It had been driven up the New Jersey Turnpike and through Manhattan to the show, becoming the event’s most Instagrammable moment.


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


Aaron Robinson


With a three-year plan in place, Neveau says the floor plan is already sketched out for next year with an increase in space and an improvement in the food. Another tweak we’d suggest: more focus on displays that make good social media posts. Paris Retromobile had the luxury of evolving before the internet, but New York Retromobile has to hustle for attention in the modern age. A hall filled with cars parked cheek-to-jowl does not make compelling social media fodder. There were some missed opportunities to combine cars—the show’s entrance had a Porsche 917, a Bugatti Atlantic, and a Ferrari 275 GTB—with the soaring architecture of Javits. The organizers could take a page from Luftgekuhlt, the Goodwood Festival of Speed, and other visually designed shows and put more effort into developing displays that will break the internet.


Meanwhile, perhaps not quite worth two whole days, the inaugural Retromobile New York was nonetheless a day or day-and-a-half of entertainment, which left plenty of time to see some of the city’s many other attractions at a time of the year when the crisp fall weather hadn’t quite lapsed into winter misery. It has many of the ingredients for success; we’ll just see if this baby can run.
